2026 SEMA Show • Nissan Returns to the Annual SEMA Show Featuring a 300-HP Sentra Spec-V Revival Concept, Two Z Cars
Dad Has Kept This 1984 Chrysler Parked for 18 Years, Wants To Pass It On to His Girl
21 photos
Photo: Detail Dane | YouTube
A car enthusiast has been keeping this 1984 Chrysler LeBaron locked in a garage years after years, just making sure that it runs and drives. He wants to preserve the car because one day, he wants to pass it on to his daughter. At the age of eight, she can already see herself driving to high school in her dad's LeBaron.
Brian has had this 1984 Chrysler LeBaron for 18 years. And all of this time, it stayed parked in the family garage, collecting dust instead of miles. When he brought the car home back in 2006, it was already used to sitting. That was exactly what it did before he purchased it: it spent 13 long years in another garage.
However, the time has come for it to hit the road again. Brian wants to prepare it for his daughter, even though she won’t be driving it anytime soon. Brian's daughter is just eight and loves the car that talks to her. It may sound very 2026-ish, but that is exactly what the LeBaron did back in 1984.
The car was equipped with the Electronic Voice Alert (EVA) system, which was Chrysler's most daring step into the 1980s space-age technology. Rather than using a simple beep or buzz, the LeBaron featured a speech synthesizer chip that made the car capable of literally talking to the driver.
Photo: Detail Dane | YouTube Sure, it was a robotic voice, but it was something other cars did not have at the time. That was long before cars told us jokes when you asked them, set the navigation to restaurants when we told them we’re hungry, or adjusted the temperature in the cabin when we let them know we’re cold.
The EVA did not say much, but it could warn the driver in an authoritative male voice, using short sentences such as " Your parking brake is on" or " A door is ajar ." However, it was a love-hate situation. For instance, if a sensor failed or a door switch got loose, the car would repeatedly cycle through warnings. Drivers grew tired of being told " A door is ajar " when driving down bumpy roads.
However, the LeBaron was the right car at the right time in an era when Chrysler needed affordable models to sell more and stay afloat in a challenging market. It was regarded as the car that made the modern front-wheel-drive convertible popular.
It came with the so-called "waterfall" grille, sporting the pattern with closely spaced, thin vertical chrome blades, opera windows on the four-door sedan and the two-door coupe. In the meantime, the convertible rolled off the production line with a folding fabric top with a rear window, upgraded from plastic to glass for the 1984 model year.
{fullimg6]
Built on Lee Iacocca’s famous K-car platform, the 1984 LeBaron also debuted the multi-point electronic fuel injection in the 2.2-liter turbocharged inline-four, which produced 140 horsepower (143 metric horsepower). The 2.2 sat at the top of the lineup.
In the meantime, the base engine was the 2.2-liter inline-four with 96 horsepower (98 metric horsepower), while the 2.6-liter Mitsubishi G54B four-cylinder produced 99 horsepower (101 metric horsepower) under the hood of the LeBaron. Buyers could go for either the five-speed Getrag manual or the three-speed automatic TorqueFlite transmission, as Brian’s car has.
Brian bought it from a friend in Glen Arbor, Michigan. The owner was Elizabeth Weaver, former Chief Justice of the Court from 1999 to 2001. She had kept it in a garage for 13 years. She stopped driving it at some point because the convertible top no longer worked. Besides, she had another little convertible that she used to drive around.
At the time, Brian was in bad need of a car, and she promised she would make a deal with him if he could fix the Chrysler. And he could. But he drove it home and parked it, planning to work on it. However, life happened, and the LeBaron has been sitting ever since.
Photo: Detail Dane | YouTube Now, he called a detailer because he wants to get it cleaned. One day, it will be his daughter’s daily driver, but that day is still very far away. His daughter is just eight. Dane of Detail Dan e loads the car onto his trailer and takes it to his studio for a makeover.
Dust and grime have gathered on the dashboard plastic, and the silver vinyl that covers the seats and door panel on board the LeBaron. So the detailing expert uses the steamer, a degreaser, microfiber towels and brushes to access all the areas and remove the dirt.
He meticulously washes the engine bay, then covers the entire body in foam to decontaminate the paint and get rid of the dust this car has collected over the years instead of collecting miles. He rubs every inch of it to agitate the dirt embedded in the paint finish and in the vinyl convertible top.
The single-stage paint, which Chrysler called Gunmetal Blue, paint code CC6, one of the most popular paint choices at the time, has completely lost its shine and has gone matte. So the only way back to its shine is polishing it.
Photo: Detail Dane | YouTube When Brian walks into the garage, he can hardly believe his eyes. " It looks like it’s on the showroom floor ," he says. His eight-year-old daughter gets in the driver’s seat. She hardly reaches the pedals, but she will be ready for the Chrysler when she is in high school.

2026 SEMA Show • 2027 Toyota Crown Signia Gets GT-S Concept Treatment for SEMA, Becomes a Sleek Wagon
1968 Mustang Hardtop Is a 1-of-1 Unicorn, Packs Super-Rare Factory Cobra Jet, and Mileage Mystery
36 photos
Photo: GTS Classic Motors
The Mustang is remembered for many things, from being a sensational new automobile that established the pony car segment (only with the name), to being one of Detroit’s hottest rods of the sixties. It was, and it has a lot on its name to brag with: Shelby GT350 and GT500, Boss 302, 429, and 351, 428 and 429 Cobra Jet. The former became a very menacing reality mid-way through 1968, in April (the Mustang’s glory month), and here’s one example to prove me right.
In the late sixties, pony cars had matured into full-fledged stallions fighting for supremacy and getting out of no one’s way, no matter how big of an engine those opponents carried, or on what platform they rolled. Chevrolet threw a 396 in the Camaro, Pontiac slammed a 400 in the Firebird, Plymouth stuffed a 383 in the Barracuda (and even a 440), AMC dropped a 390 in the Javelin, all the while Dodge‘s Challenger didn’t bother to exist before 1970.
Ford, on the other hand, was caught slightly off-foot at first, getting the Mustang armed with big-block might with 390 cubic inches fairly late, in ‘67, despite having far better and bigger engines available. However, FoMoCo also had a standing agreement with Shelby American, and the 428 cubic inches in the Police Interceptor from 1967 was plenty go-fast swagger.
And then, Ford decided to throw a curve ball at the very man who led the Blue Oval to Le Mans glory, and threw Shelby’s cobra badge under the bus with a Cobra Jet.
Photo: GTS Classic Motors When Ford unleashed the 428 Cobra Jet midway through the 1968 model year, the Dearborn camp finally possessed a lethal weapon to combat rival big-blocks on street and strip alike. The mid-year introduction, historically classified as the 1968 ½ (in line with Ford’s long-standing tradition of “and-a-halves”), achieved instant motorsport folklore by sweeping the 1968 NHRA Winternationals in Pomona.
While the swooping fastback model took nearly all the historical acclaim, the understated two-door hardtop coupe carried that identical thunderous punch beneath its formal notchback roofline.
Muscle motoring enthusiasts who stepped up to buy Ford's brutal R-code engine option overwhelmingly chose the athletic fastback shape, turning the hardtop into an exceptionally scarce oddity. Dearborn assembly lines completed just 221 units of the 1968 1/2 Ford Mustang GT coupe carrying the 428-cubic inch Cobra Jet V8.
By comparison, Ford built 1,044 fastback brethren and a mere 37 convertibles, cementing this hardtop as one of the rarest high-performance production Mustangs to leave the factory.
Photo: GTS Classic Motors Ben Shearman, the boss of GTS Classic Motors out of Waterford, Pennsylvania, recently offered a look at an authentic survivor of this low-production breed on the eponymous YouTube channel. Bathed in factory Code T Candyapple Red paint and wearing its mandatory satin black hood stripe, the car stands as an ultimate undercover street brawler. Casual observers at weekend gatherings usually mistake it for a modest small-block daily driver until the burly 7.0-liter FE V8 fires to life.
Shearman is well acquainted with this particular notchback, having owned the pony car several years back before selling it to a family in central Pennsylvania. When those owners decided to travel and part with the coupe after three years, Shearman jumped at the chance to reacquire it. While towing it home with his trailer, an unexpected bearing failure altered the plan, forcing Shearman to drive the car 140 miles (225 km) on Interstate 90 at 65 mph (105 kph).
Unlike touchy concourse showpieces that live solely atop trailers, this genuine R-code performed with impeccable mechanical poise, running cool, tracking straight, and shifting effortlessly through each gear. Naturally, the thirsty big-block demanded three pit stops across that distance – and it wasn’t to change tires, or drivers. That big Holley perched atop an iron intake is the monetary equivalent of plasma cutters, gashing wallets like Japanese sushi masters fileting blue-finned tuna.
Photo: GTS Classic Motors Back in Waterford, the GTS Classic Motors team completed a full service, applying heavy-zinc 20W-50 oil and marine-grade grease across the chassis. Not too bad, for a car showing 2,981 miles on the odometer. There is a catch, though, but you’ll have to take it up to Ben himself and inquire about that odometer reading.
Ford officially advertised the 428 Cobra Jet at a modest 335 hp (340 PS) and 440 lb-ft (597 Nm) of torque to outmaneuver escalating insurance rates. The actual dynamometer figure hovered comfortably at 410 hp (406 PS), bolstered by 427-style high-flow cylinder heads, a 735-cfm Holley four-barrel carburetor, and beefier main bearing webs.
Mated to a heavy-duty C6 three-speed automatic transmission and a 3.50:1 Traction-Lok rear axle, the powertrain Ford’s first warning shot in the factory-armed pony horsepower wars.
Photo: GTS Classic Motors The Candyapple Red finish recently received extensive multi-stage paint correction, bringing back deep mirror-like gloss across all original sheet metal. Proper GT styled steel wheels feature factory-spec chrome trim rings, center caps, and period-correct F70-14 Goodyear Polyglas bias-ply tires mounted and balanced at Shearman's dealership.
The body structure exhibits clean integrity, retaining solid floor pans, trunk drop-offs, and inner fender aprons, along with the original factory transport tie-down decal affixed beneath the rear bumper.
Inside the passenger compartment, the standard factory black vinyl interior showcases remarkably crisp seating surfaces, original lap safety belts, tinted Carlite glass, and a full center console. An original Philco AM push-button radio sits cleanly inside the dash panel, accompanied by fully functional original gauges, indicators, and courtesy lamps.
Photo: YouTube/GTS Classic Motors The original buyer thoughtfully selected factory power front disc brakes and power steering, giving this heavyweight muscle machine remarkably civilized, compliant, and stress-free road manners that are still up to the job of modern traffic.
Lifting the steel hood reveals an authentic engine bay treated to precise factory details, including correct date-coded spark plug wires, a period Autolite coil, and surviving assembly inspection marks. Along the door data plate and dashboard VIN tag, a framed Elite Marti Report testifies to this Mustang’s authenticity. The Marti documentation confirms that this exact equipment combination, mixing Code T paint with black trim and a console, makes the car a bona fide 1-of-1 build.
While fastback models continually dominate the headlines at major classic car auctions, an authentic 1968 1/2 Mustang GT hardtop coupe offers a far more elusive and stealthier alternative. The car benefits from an older restoration that has settled into sweet running order, completely free of irritating teething troubles or unfinished mechanical quirks.
If you made it to this point and didn’t stop wondering what the asking price might be, the dealer can help with that detail. Just out of professional curiosity, what do you think it’s worth, just by looking at the photos and watching the video embedded below?

2026 SEMA Show • Toyota Puts Snow Tracks on Five SUVs and Trucks, Unloads Them at SEMA 2026 as the Snowhunter Bunch
Eye Candy 1960 Plymouth Fury Is a Tribute to Owner's Dad, Won Best of Show at First Outing
71 photos
Photo: YouTube/Lou Costabile
“Why this car of all the cars?” “I mean, look at it! It’s like jewelry!” They say diamonds are a girl’s best friends. By rise of hand, how many of you have ever driven a diamond? Didn’t think so. Besides, a diamond is good for two things: shine and cut glass, all the while being obnoxiously expensive. If you find that infuriating, take your Fury to the next car meet. If it wins Best of Show, then maybe this 1960 Plymouth Fury will spark your interest.
When Chrysler Corporation stylist Virgil Exner unleashed his "Forward Look" design language in 1955, Plymouth rapidly shed its staid, utilitarian reputation for bold aerodynamic flair. That stylistic revolution birthed the Plymouth Fury in 1956, a limited-production halo coupe built on a 115-inch (2,921 mm) wheelbase and measuring 204.8 inches (5,202 mm) overall. Finished exclusively in Sand Dune White with anodized gold aluminum trim, the debut Fury totaled 4,485 units at its premiere.
Priced at $2,866, that inaugural 1956 hardtop carried a 303-cubic-inch (5.0-liter) Polyspherical V8 rated at 240 hp (243 PS) and 310 lb-ft (420 Nm), famously clocking 143.596 mph (231.096 kph) at Daytona Beach. Stretched onto a 118-inch (2,997 mm) wheelbase for 1957, the Fury gained a 290-hp (294-PS) 318-cubic-inch (5.2-liter) V8 across 7,438 cars, while the 1958 edition offered a 305-hp (309-PS) 350-cubic-inch (5.7-liter) V8 across 5,303 total examples.
By 1959, Plymouth elevated the Fury into a full-fledged top-tier trim line totaling 65,257 cars alongside 23,857 upscale Sport Fury models. For 1960, the Sport Fury badge vanished, consolidating all flagship models under the Fury banner just as Chrysler Corporation introduced unitized construction, replacing body-on-frame paradigms in favor of 5,400 weld spots.
Photo: YouTube/Lou Costabile That watershed 1960 lineup also debuted the 383-cubic-inch (6.3-liter) Sonoramic Commando cross-ram V8, delivering 330 hp (335 PS) and 460 lb-ft (624 Nm).
Measuring 209.4 inches (5,319 mm) in length, 78.6 inches (1,996 mm) in width, and 54.6 inches (1,387 mm) in height, the 1960 Fury accounted for 63,073 of the 483,969 vehicles Plymouth produced that model year, including 18,079 pillarless two-door hardtop coupes priced $2,717 and up, depending on optional extras.
Because premature corrosion claimed most early unibody Mopars, surviving representatives of that model year are remarkably scarce. That’s what makes the example featured by YouTuber Lou Costabile on his channel a show piece extraordinaire. That, and the fact Michelle, its owner, chose it as her nostalgic throwback forget-me-not to her dad.
This striking 1960 Plymouth Fury two-door hardtop entered Michelle’s life in 2025, and Lou first spotted the car at a regional show where the classic Mopar captured Best of Show honors. In a foreshadowing encounter, the YouTuber laid eyes on the car and complimented the owner for being the one who “brought a real car” to the meet. That was before the judges chose the Fury as the star of the event.
Photo: YouTube/Lou Costabile Michelle developed her affinity for full-size American iron through her father, whose work car allowance brought a rotating fleet of Chevrolets, Buicks, Lincoln Continentals, and Chryslers into the family driveway. She earned her learner's permit piloting a limousine-sized Chrysler New Yorker, cementing her lifelong preference for land yachts. After buying the Fury, she joined the Revved Up Women's Car Club of Lockport, Illinois, at a local show.
When Michelle first inspected the 3,535-pound (1,603-kilogram) hardtop in 2025, she hoped she would not fall as hard for it as she anticipated, yet its brightwork immediately reminded her of fine jewelry.
(I must say, I never thought of that before, but she’s got a point. Car girls always see more than men, I don’t care how seasoned they may be, how many knuckles they bust wrenching, or how many miles they covered at the steering wheel. I woman will dismiss or back all that expertise in half a blink of an eye, and she’d be right either way).
Photo: YouTube/Lou Costabile The two-tone red and white exterior of this 51,400-mile gem showcases quad headlamps, a horizontal-blade aluminum grille bearing a gold rocket emblem (actually a stylized “Mayflower,” the ship that brought the settlers from Europe to Plymouth Rock), front fender spears, white coves with gold Fury script, Kelsey-Hayes wire wheels, wide whitewalls, and ribbed chrome rear fender skirts.
I really want to meet the car designer that can match this in 2026 (Don’t say Giugiaro, he’s been penning masterpieces since when beauties like this ’60 Fury were new, and he’s proven his mastery over and over again – and continues to do it today). In fact, if you can think of a car made in the past two decades that can match the styling of this Fury, I’ll gladly do a feature story on it. the comments section is yours.
Crowning the rear quarters are Exner's canted stabilizer tailfins, each wearing a red, white, and blue roundel that echoes the aerospace motifs of 1960, just as America was building steam for the Space Race. Between those towering blades sits the optional Sport Deck lid with its simulated spare tire stamping. Inside the trunk, beside the real whitewall spare, Michelle keeps a 1960 owner's manual, an accessories booklet, and a Virginia dealer prestige sales catalog.
Photo: YouTube/Lou Costabile Decoding the factory plates reveals fascinating provenance behind this Mopar. The door-jamb serial number confirms a 1960 V8 Fury built at the Newark, Delaware plant. Under the hood, the cowl tag lists shipping order 1230 for December 30, 1959, body code 332, trim code 123, and paint code YY2, showing it originally wore two-tone Caramel Metallic/Desert Beige lower body paint over a Caramel/Brown Vinyl and Black Cloth interior upholstery exclusive to the 1960 Fury series.
I firmly believe the current red/white with red-white-and-black theme is one million times better looking than the original, but that’s just personal preference. What’s not up to subjective debate is lying underhood. Plymouth's dependable 318-cubic-inch (5.2-liter) Fury V-800 Polyspherical engine, finished in red with a gold intake manifold and a red air cleaner.
It’s the famous 318 Poly, which stood on the market for a brief decade (1957-1966); not to be confused with the later 318 LA that succeeded it as the go-to small-block Mopar V8. Featuring a 9.0:1 compression ratio and mechanical lifters, the standard two-barrel version generated 230 hp (233 PS) at 4,400 rpm and 340 lb-ft (461 Nm) at 2,400 rpm, whereas the four-barrel Super Pak delivered 260 hp (264 PS) and 345 lb-ft (468 Nm) of torque.
Photo: YouTube/Lou Costabile There was a dual-quad iteration, the V-800, offered for a brief two years (’57-’58), rated at 290 hp (293 PS) and 330 lb-ft (421 Nm).
Inside the pillarless cabin, the restored tri-tone red, white, and black upholstery pairs patterned black cloth inserts with vinyl bolsters and a padded driver-side backrest crest. Facing the driver is Plymouth's flattened Aero steering wheel with translucent sparkle-flecked Lucite rims framing a 120-mph (193-kph) ribbon speedometer.
Five push buttons on the left control the TorqueFlite automatic, while push-button climate controls, an AM radio, and a clock complete the period dash. The brightwork is blinding – and that’s not always a metaphor, but that was 1960s motoring for you – sparkling in every single detail, from the tip of the front bumper to the exhaust pipes.
Wearing red boots and a matching red purse, Michelle guides the Fury out on the highway, where the Torsion-Aire suspension delivers a magic-carpet glide as it passes a vintage Ford Model A pickup, making the driver wave and smile at the sight of the rolling piece of jewelry.

2026 SEMA Show • Nissan Returns to the Annual SEMA Show Featuring a 300-HP Sentra Spec-V Revival Concept, Two Z Cars
Mattel Brick Shop Racer Series Is the Next Big Thing for Hot Wheels Collectors in 2027
30 photos
Photo: Instagram/User ddcollectibles
I’m dreaming of the moment when I’ll be able to indulge in multiple forms of motorsports all within the same year. I’d be drifting my FC RX-7 one week, going into Time Attack mode in an FD the following one, and then rallying in a first-gen RX-7 on the next occasion.
And yes, I’d find something to do with the RX-8 as well: I would most likely use it to give other people their first dose of driving at the track, as it’s quite a bit more user friendly than either one of the RX-7s.
The problem with this kind of diversity is that it would be financially exhausting unless I’d have at least half a million dollars in my bank account. So until I get there (if ever), my only chance is to focus on sim racing and tiny scale model cars to keep me happy.
However, you should always be aware of the situations you’re getting yourself into. Something that might look affordable at first could prove to be a financial nightmare beyond a certain point. And yes, you can experience that sort of trouble even when dealing with Hot Wheels collectibles.
I’ve said this many times before, and it’s the kind of warning that can save you a lot of trouble further down the road. By now most of you may already know that starting last year, there’s a new way to collect and play with Hot Wheels .
Photo: Mattel The Mattel Brick Shop series is the company’s way to get a share of the market that Lego most certainly controls, even though there are quite a few players out there trying to reach for the top.
We unboxed and built a Maserati MC20 almost one year ago, but I confess I haven’t bought a single item in the series until now. It’s not just because it has been scarcely available where I’m at, or because of the fact that I don’t typically have the time to build them.
Pricing has been an issue, too. Instead of getting the smaller, 1:32nd-scale collectibles, I could buy two to three Premium 1/64th-scale Hot Wheels . Moving into the 1:16th-scale category, those can be worth more than an entire Car Culture set.
And if you really want the biggest of challenges, the 1:12th-scale items can cost as much as three Premium sets. I keep saying I’ll buy one for Christmas, and I’m currently undecided between the Toyota Supra and the Acura NSX.
Photo: Instagram/User DDcollectibles Anyway, I can tell how sales are going just by how many discounted offers the dealers in my area have resorted to in attempt to clear their stock. I don’t think it’s going as planned, not in this economy. Mattel wasn’t just going to give up on the idea, though.
It’s a clear case of “Improvise, adapt, overcome” as the series takes on a new shape with the Racer Series. Yes, Mattel Brick Shop cars already had a 1/64th-scale Hot Wheels inside, but it wasn’t a buildable model.
That’s what the company is aiming for now, and it seems we’ll be getting 20 of them throughout the year. You’ll find photos of the first six ones, and it seems the manufacturer is betting big on Chase collectibles again.
The Bone Shaker will be the first one and I can only assume the special car will have a different paint job to set it apart. The piece count for each vehicle varies between 27 to 29, which is fairly impressive considering how small these are.
Photo: Instagram/User DDcollectibles You still get the thrill of building it yourself, but it only takes minutes to get the job done with easy-to-read instructions on a piece of paper inside the box. This preview shows how to build the white Honda S2000 , and I have to say it looks better than the 1:32nd-scale version.
I have mixed feelings about the wheels right now, as they’re certainly different from what you get in the Mainline or Silver Series. However, it’s much too early for the final verdict.
The person that published the photos even brought out the Super Treasure Hunt version (AEM Power) of Ryu Asada’s old casting for a comparison. There are some limitations that come with the brick-building process, as you’d expect, but the result is still quite impressive.
Chances are Mattel will proceed the same way it did with Elite 64: give us all new castings for at least one year (if not two), before coming back with recolors to account for the licensing fees.
Photo: Instagram/User DDcollectibles If you want my estimate on the price, I’d say it has to be lower than $10 to reel collectors in. If these can be at the same level or cheaper than the Car Culture/Boulevard collectibles, they’re bound to succeed. We won’t know for sure until December or January, though.
While the Honda S2000 is #5 of 20 for next year, the '24 Camaro ZL1 is the first in line. It’s the only licensed, American model on the list so far, unless you feel the ‘91 Acura NSX belongs there too.
Europe is off to a good start with the ‘18 Audi TT RS and the Maserati MCPura. That last one is an interesting choice for sure, especially since we don’t have it in any other series from the El Segundo-based manufacturer so far.
Looking at the blister packaging you can clearly tell you’re dealing with a building set, and I just hope the graphics are an accurate reflection of the final product. Now I’m off to order that Supra as I can’t stand waiting any further for it.

Eli Electric Vehicles is getting ready to reveal a new version of its tiny electric microcar, and this one could expand its usefulness beyond the slow lane.
In an Instagram teaser ahead of EICMA in Milan, the company announced the upcoming Eli ZERO MX, describing it as a new L7e vehicle joining its lineup. Eli also teased a special Race Edition, with promotional artwork showing a dark, sporty-looking ZERO with red accents and a visibly open-sided cabin.
The teaser doesn’t give us much to go on in terms of hard and fast details, but the L7e designation is the biggest clue here.
The familiar European Eli ZERO that we test-drove a few years ago is an L6e light quadricycle, with a top speed of 45 km/h (28 mph). Its compact two-seat layout makes it an appealing urban runabout, though that speed ceiling limits its usefulness on faster roads. But L7e vehicles can typically travel at speeds of up to 80-90 km/h (50-56 mph).
Advertisement - scroll for more content
A faster version could make the little EV practical for considerably more trips. And there’s already a tantalizing hint: Eli’s Italian website lists an L7e ZERO capable of 85 km/h (53 mph), with a claimed range of up to 200 km (124 miles). Whether those specifications directly describe the upcoming ZERO MX remains unconfirmed by the teaser.
If they do, that would suggest a much more versatile commuter while retaining the tiny footprint that makes these vehicles so easy to park.
View this post on Instagram
The Race Edition raises a different set of questions. The new vehicle could feature a sportier design, such as race seats and alternative doors. That could point toward a playful or more tuned vehicle, though we’ll have to wait to learn whether “Race” means additional performance or primarily a styling package.
It’s also unclear how closely the Race Edition and ZERO MX are related. The caption presents them separately, while the artwork additionally points towards a second-generation ZERO.
Either way, a roughly 50 mph Eli would be an interesting proposition: still small enough to rethink how much vehicle a daily commute requires, but potentially fast enough to cover routes the original couldn’t comfortably handle.
Eli says the reveal takes place at EICMA, November 3–8, in Hall 22, Stand B40. We’ll be there to see what they unveil.

This 1966 Dodge Charger Looks Too Good To Be Left in a Junkyard, Full Restoration Needed
23 photos
Photo: eBay seller missvoidvixen93
Runs and drives. Easy restoration project. These are just some of the words the owner of this 1966 Dodge Charger uses to describe the car they posted online specifically to look for a new home.
This is a project that looks like it’s been parked outside, next to other projects and under the clear sky. This can’t be good news for a vehicle that’s still in good shape, and because it needs a complete restoration, the more it sits, the more difficult it is to return to the road in tip-top shape.
The owner says the vehicle is still complete, and this is fantastic news for someone planning a complete restoration. Theoretically, at least without seeing the car in person, this means that you should be able to turn it into a daily driver without spending much time online to look for parts.
As for the engine under the hood, this Charger was born with a 361 but is now powered by a 440 paired with an automatic transmission.
The engine lineup in 1966 was the 318 rated at 230 horsepower, while the 361 was the first optional unit on the list. It produced 265 horsepower and was a well-balanced option for buyers who wanted a little bit more power than the standard engine but without spending too many dollars on something that burns fuel non-stop.
The 383 was a popular option with 330 horsepower, while the top choice was the one and the only Hemi rated at 425 horsepower.
While this Charger is now fitted with a 440, I wish we knew more about the engine. It does start and run, so it’s technically in good shape, we don’t have more specifics, such as the model year that donated it and whether it has ever been rebuilt.
This Charger is surprisingly solid for a project, and the cabin looks impressive for a car that has been sitting in the owner’s yard, trying to sell and eventually get a complete restoration. I believe that checking it out in person is still the recommended approach, especially considering that someone who might be planning to attempt a complete restoration needs more information, including about the condition of the metal.
If possible, you should raise this Charger on a lift to check the undersides and obviously inspect the trunk before even thinking of making an offer.
Otherwise, you just need to be ready for a hefty price tag. The owner believes that $29,500 is a fair price, but they also enabled the Make Offer option on eBay, so maybe you can get a better deal with the right negotiation skills.
The vehicle is parked in Florissant, Colorado, and you should be able to drive it home if you don’t live far from this location.

Radiance Park Model Tiny Home Elevates Tiny Living With a Spacious Layout and Modern Amenities
24 photos
Photo: Cavco Industries
Rising real estate prices and high borrowing costs make traditional homeownership hard to achieve for many individuals and families. So the idea of downsizing has emerged as a beacon of home for those who want a home to call their own with less debt and more financial freedom.
Today's tiny houses come in all shapes and sizes, but if you want a home that still feels residential, there is no better small living option than a park model tiny house. Larger and wider than regular tiny homes on wheels but still transportable, park model RVs are a great middle ground between a traditional RV and a brick-and-mortar conventional home.
If it’s not mobility you’re looking for in particular, but rather a simplified lifestyle in a smaller home that still offers enough room for more people to coexist comfortably, a park model tiny home like the Radiance might be what you need.
Designed and built by well-known US manufacturer Cavco Industries, the Radiance park model is not meant for extreme downsizing. This model takes the simplicity and efficiency of tiny living and elevates it with modern amenities, an efficient floor plan that prioritizes comfort and openness, and stylish finishes.
Photo: Cavco Industries Measuring 34.2 feet (10.4 meters) long and 11.4 feet (3.4 meters) wide, it offers 400 square feet (37 square meters) of living space, which is enough to accommodate a more traditional layout and living arrangement, with standard furniture, residential-style appliances, a main-floor bedroom, and a full-size kitchen and bathroom.
Both the interior and exterior of this tiny house are modern but exude the warmth and charm of a mini-cottage. On the outside, for instance, the home is finished with olive green lap siding, black trim around the white windows, and a slightly pitched metal roof. Transom windows are another notable exterior feature, allowing natural light to get in while also contributing to the cottage-like appearance.
A large sliding glass patio door invites you inside, where you’ll be surprised by how open, home-like, and inviting the Radiance is. With enough room for proper cooking, spelling, and gathering spaces,it instantly feels more familiar and cozy than what many people expect from a tiny house. And with not one but two bedrooms - a private one downstairs and a sleeping loft - it could also serve as a family home.
Photo: Cavco Industries The entry door opens directly into the front kitchen area, which, thanks to the wider footprint of the house, is quite spacious and very well configured for daily use. Not to mention, it also integrates a wood-top kitchen island that doubles as a dining area for at least four people.
Boasting an L-shape design, the culinary space is fitted with black upper and lower cabinets, a tiled backsplash, and a white countertop. A full suite of residential appliances give the kitchen the familiar setup of a conventional home, making cooking a pleasure. This includes a refrigerator, a full gas range with a range hood, and a farmhouse-style stainless steel sink. Cavco Homes has recently started to leave out the dishwasher and microwave from the kitchen setup, but there is enough room for owners to later add these appliances if they want to.
Just like the kitchen, the adjacent living room also makes you forget you’re inside a tiny house . There is space for a proper sofa, an armchair, and a coffee table, along with an entertainment wall with a TV and fireplace, creating a proper space for gatherings and relaxation.
Photo: Cavco Industries The electric fireplace is surrounded by rustic, light-gray faux stone, while the upper section features dark vertical shiplap. Two vertical windows frame the entertainment wall, bringing in plenty of natural light and providing views of the outdoors.
The rest of the house is dedicated to the sleeping quarters and the bathroom, and it feels more private. As mentioned, the Radiance park model has two separate bedrooms, which makes it quite versatile. The master bedroom on the ground floor is completely private and comes fully furnished with a comfortable queen bed, nightstands, open upper cubbies, and a large wardrobe. There is also space for a TV on the wall, and a large window keeps the space luminous.
The loft above this bedroom is accessed via an easy-to-climb, carpeted staircase with a safety railing. It is a typical loft with lower ceilings but it’s large enough to accommodate a queen mattress or two twins, offering additional sleeping space for guests or family.
Photo: Cavco Industries The three-piece bathroom is decently sized and features a white porcelain gravity-flush toilet, a large glass-enclosed shower, and an elongated vanity with a cabinet and open shelves for storage. A wall-mounted linen cabinet and a mirrored medicine cabinet are also included.
Like many park model tiny houses, the Radiance needs to be parked somewhere with proper utility connections, as it draws power through a standard RV-style hookup.
Built on a heavy-duty triple-axle trailer, the Radiance meets residential construction codes, with high-end residential materials like finished drywall, steel I-beams, and robust insulation. It’s factory-built and transported to its destination in one piece, and it’s destined for permanent or semi-permanent placement at a campground, RV resort, or on private land.
Spacious, comfortable, and stylish, the Radiance park model tiny is a great option for people interested in tiny home living but reluctant to give up the familiarity of a traditional house. Pricing depends on the configuration you choose and your dealer.

Is This Chevy 210 Worth Nearly $60K? A Dealer Says It Is, Uses a Beautiful Color To Convince You
40 photos
Photo: West Coast Classics
While Bel Airs are particularly desirable whenever people are in the market for 1957 Chevys, this 210 is here to prove there’s more to discover beyond the top configuration.
The car has already been restored and upgraded, so it’s now trying to find a new home in a condition that doesn’t require any other investments. This makes sense, as the vehicle is in perfect shape, and I can’t help but insist on the beautiful paint.
The paint job looks fantastic, and I believe that the photos don’t do enough justice. Potential buyers should just go check it out in person, and the chances are that they’ll be impressed once they see it live.
As the last year of the Tri-Five, the 1957 Chevy release came down to the same three models as in previous years. The Bel Air was the top configuration, while the 150 was the most affordable model for people who just wanted a cheap car capable of doing everything, without spending much on maintenance or luxury items.
The 210 was somewhere in the middle, being offered with the same engine options as the Bel Air. Chevrolet introduced the 283 V8 engine in 1957, with a two-barrel version serving as the entry into this new lineup. However, the 283 was also available in several other configurations, including a four-barrel unit and a fuel-injected setup that was particularly troubling in terms of reliability.
This car no longer has the original engine under the hood, but this is hardly a surprise. Many classic Chevys end up getting small blocks, and this is also the case with this 1957 210, as it’s now powered by a 350ci V8 engine. It is paired with a 4-speed automatic transmission, and while no further specifics were shared, it’s safe to assume that it starts, runs, and drives properly.
The car is also fitted with air conditioning, power steering, and power 4-wheel disc brakes. It goes without saying that this 210 has already stepped away from its all-original setup, but this isn’t necessarily a reason to walk away if you know what these custom builds are all about. A 350 is a very common upgrade on classic Chevys, and given the condition of this car, it’s safe to assume that restoring this 210 wasn’t necessarily a cheap job.
I would love to get more information about the paint, so if you decide to call the dealer and arrange an in-person inspection, please take some pics and share it with me.
Otherwise, it might be hard for this 210 to convince buyers to pay that much for it. The dealer wants $59,500, and if you want to go there in person, you can find it in Torrence, California.
